Task and constraints: Given an array of intervals where intervals[i] = [starti, endi], merge all overlapping intervals, and return an array of the non-overlapping intervals that cover all the intervals in the input. The method returns the requested result for the stated input format.
Idea: Sorts intervals by their starts, then appends disjoint intervals or extends the last result interval when the next interval overlaps.
Technique and why it applies: Sorting plus a single sweep makes overlapping intervals adjacent.
Invariant: result contains merged intervals for all intervals processed so far.
Edge cases: Touching endpoints merge. Sorting mutates the input and result entries can alias original interval lists.
Complexity: The author labels time O(nlogn) and space O(1); Time is O(n log n) for sorting and O(n) for scanning; result storage is O(n), excluding input.

Task and constraints: You are given an array of non-overlapping intervals intervals where intervals[i] = [starti, endi] represent the start and the end of the i^th interval and intervals is sorted in ascending order by starti. You are also given an interval newInterval = [start, end] that represents the start and end of another interval. The method returns the requested result for the stated input format.
Idea: Appends newInterval to the input, sorts all intervals by start, then appends disjoint intervals or merges overlaps into the last result entry.
Technique and why it applies: Sorting then sweeping handles overlaps in start order.
Invariant: result contains merged intervals for the sorted prefix already processed.
Edge cases: The input list is modified by append and sort; touching intervals merge. The result may reuse inner interval lists.
Complexity: No author label was supplied. Time is O(n log n) because of sorting; result space is O(n).

Task and constraints: You are given an array of non-overlapping intervals intervals where intervals[i] = [starti, endi] represent the start and the end of the i^th interval and intervals is sorted in ascending order by starti. You are also given an interval newInterval = [start, end] that represents the start and end of another interval. The method returns the requested result for the stated input format.
Idea: Copies intervals that end before newInterval begins, merges all overlapping intervals into newInterval, appends it, then extends with the remaining suffix.
Technique and why it applies: A linear sweep fits when the original intervals are already sorted and non-overlapping.
Invariant: result holds completed intervals before the insertion; newInterval accumulates every overlapping interval.
Edge cases: Intervals touching at endpoints merge. The code slices intervals[i:] and builds a new merged list; it assumes input intervals are already ordered and non-overlapping.
Complexity: The author labels O(n) time and O(1) space; time is O(n), but result and the suffix extension require O(n) output space, excluding output conventions.

Task and constraints: Given a string s consisting of words and spaces, return the length of the last word in the string. The method returns the requested result for the stated input format.
Idea: Strips outer whitespace, splits the string on whitespace or literal spaces, and returns the length of the final token.
Technique and why it applies: String trimming and splitting locate the last word directly.
Invariant: The final split token is treated as the last word after trimming.
Edge cases: The two variants differ: split() collapses whitespace, while split(' ') can leave empty tokens between repeated spaces. Temporary strings and a list are allocated.
Complexity: Time is O(n); space is O(n) because strip/split materialize strings and tokens.

Task and constraints: Given a string s consisting of words and spaces, return the length of the last word in the string. The method returns the requested result for the stated input format.
Idea: Scans characters from right to left, counting non-space characters and stops at the first space after counting begins.
Technique and why it applies: Reverse scanning finds the final word without splitting the whole string.
Invariant: length counts characters in the suffix after trailing spaces and within the last word.
Edge cases: Trailing spaces are ignored; all spaces return zero. Only the literal space character is treated as a separator.
Complexity: The author labels time O(n) and space O(1); Time is O(n) and auxiliary space O(1), as each character is visited at most once.

Task and constraints: Given a positive integer n, generate an n x n matrix filled with elements from 1 to n^2 in spiral order. The method returns the requested result for the stated input format.
Idea: Creates an n by n zero matrix, then fills the top row, right column, bottom row and left column for each layer while incrementing the next value.
Technique and why it applies: Boundary simulation places consecutive values in spiral order.
Invariant: The four boundaries enclose the unfilled inner square after each layer.
Edge cases: n=0 returns [] in the first variant; the other also constructs an empty matrix. Boundary checks avoid overwriting cells in the center.
Complexity: Time is O(n^2); the matrix output itself uses O(n^2) space, despite labels that may count only auxiliary space.

Task and constraints: The set [1, 2, 3, ..., n] contains a total of n! unique permutations. The method returns the requested result for the stated input format.
Idea: Builds the available numbers 1..n and factorial values, converts k to zero-based indexing, then repeatedly selects the factorial-block index, removes that number, and updates k to the remainder.
Technique and why it applies: Factorial number-system indexing skips whole blocks of permutations instead of generating them.
Invariant: At each step, k identifies the requested permutation's rank among arrangements of the remaining numbers.
Edge cases: The input rank must be within the valid permutation range. nums.pop(index) shifts later elements and the output concatenates chosen numbers.
Complexity: No author label was supplied. Factorial setup is O(n); repeated indexed removals make total time O(n^2), with O(n) storage.

Task and constraints: There is a robot on an m x n grid. The robot is initially located at the top-left corner (i.e., grid[0][0]). The robot tries to move to the bottom-right corner (i.e., grid[m - 1][n - 1]). The robot can only move either down or right at any point in time. The method returns the requested result for the stated input format.
Idea: Initializes every grid cell to one, then fills interior cells with the sum of paths from above and left.
Technique and why it applies: Dynamic programming adds counts from the only two allowed predecessor cells.
Invariant: dp[i][j] stores the number of paths to that cell.
Edge cases: A single row or column has one path; positive dimensions are assumed. The full grid is allocated.
Complexity: No author label was supplied. Time and space are O(m*n), from the table and nested interior updates.

Task and constraints: There is a robot on an m x n grid. The robot is initially located at the top-left corner (i.e., grid[0][0]). The robot tries to move to the bottom-right corner (i.e., grid[m - 1][n - 1]). The robot can only move either down or right at any point in time. The method returns the requested result for the stated input format.
Idea: Keeps a one-dimensional DP array initialized to one. For each row, each later column adds the count from its left to the count already stored from above.
Technique and why it applies: Rolling-row DP reuses the previous row while updating left to right.
Invariant: dp[j] before update is the count from above; dp[j-1] is the current row's left count.
Edge cases: Single row/column returns one. The code swaps dimensions so the array uses the smaller dimension.
Complexity: The author labels O(m*n) time and O(min(m,n)) space, matching the nested loops and one row.

Task and constraints: There is a robot on an m x n grid. The robot is initially located at the top-left corner (i.e., grid[0][0]). The robot tries to move to the bottom-right corner (i.e., grid[m - 1][n - 1]). The robot can only move either down or right at any point in time. The method returns the requested result for the stated input format.
Idea: Computes a binomial coefficient using a multiplicative loop, choosing the smaller of r and n-r, and returns C(m+n-2,n-1).
Technique and why it applies: Combinatorics counts the placements of down and right moves without enumerating paths.
Invariant: The running product divided at each step maintains the exact binomial coefficient for the processed factors.
Edge cases: m or n equal to 1 gives one path. Python integers can grow large; the grid dimensions are positive.
Complexity: The author labels O(m+n) time and O(1) space; the loop runs O(min(m,n)) iterations and uses scalar variables.

Task and constraints: You are given an m x n integer array grid. There is a robot initially located at the top-left corner (i.e., grid[0][0]). The robot tries to move to the bottom-right corner (i.e., grid[m-1][n-1]). The robot can only move either down or right at any point in time. The method returns the requested result for the stated input format.
Idea: Builds a full DP grid, initializes the start to zero if blocked and one otherwise, then adds counts from an unblocked cell above and left when those predecessors are valid.
Technique and why it applies: Grid DP sums paths from the only allowed predecessor directions while excluding obstacles.
Invariant: dp[r][c] is the number of obstacle-free paths reaching that cell.
Edge cases: If the start is blocked, its initial count is zero. The code assumes a nonempty rectangular grid as guaranteed.
Complexity: No author label was supplied. Time and space are O(m*n), because it visits each cell and allocates a full grid.

Task and constraints: You are given an m x n integer array grid. There is a robot initially located at the top-left corner (i.e., grid[0][0]). The robot tries to move to the bottom-right corner (i.e., grid[m-1][n-1]). The robot can only move either down or right at any point in time. The method returns the requested result for the stated input format.
Idea: Uses one row of path counts. It resets the first column when an obstacle occurs, sets any obstacle cell to zero, and otherwise adds the count from the left to the count carried from above.
Technique and why it applies: Rolling-row grid DP keeps only the previous row and current row's left neighbor.
Invariant: ways[j] represents paths from above until updated, then accumulates the left contribution for the current row.
Edge cases: An obstacle at the start zeroes the start count; an obstacle blocks all paths through that cell. Input is nonempty by constraints.
Complexity: The author labels O(m*n) time and O(m+n) space, but the code uses O(n) auxiliary space for ways, excluding the input grid.

Task and constraints: Given a m x n grid filled with non-negative numbers, find a path from top left to bottom right, which minimizes the sum of all numbers along its path. The method returns the requested result for the stated input format.
Idea: Processes each row using a fresh temporary row. For each cell it adds the cell value to the previous-row cost and left cost, using 1000 as a boundary penalty, then keeps the smaller.
Technique and why it applies: Dynamic programming compares the only two predecessor directions, down-from-above and right-from-left.
Invariant: temp[j] is the minimum cost to reach the current cell in the current row; prev stores the row above.
Edge cases: The code assumes nonempty grid and uses 1000 as a sentinel, which is safe only because stated grid dimensions and values keep valid path sums below it.
Complexity: No author label was supplied. Time is O(m*n); space is O(n) for prev and temp, not O(m+n) unless the input/output conventions count differently.

Task and constraints: Given a m x n grid filled with non-negative numbers, find a path from top left to bottom right, which minimizes the sum of all numbers along its path. The method returns the requested result for the stated input format.
Idea: Initializes a one-dimensional array with the first row's cumulative sums, then updates the first column and each later cell using the minimum of the left and above path costs.
Technique and why it applies: In-place row DP keeps the cheapest path cost to each cell.
Invariant: sum[j] is the minimum path sum to the current row's column j after each update.
Edge cases: The grid is nonempty and values are nonnegative; the variable name sum shadows Python's built-in sum but does not affect this code.
Complexity: The author labels O(m*n) time and O(m+n) space; the code uses O(n) auxiliary storage plus the input grid.

Task and constraints: A valid number can be split up into these components (in order): The method returns the requested result for the stated input format.
Idea: Classifies each character as whitespace, sign, digit, dot or exponent and moves through a transition table; invalid transitions immediately return false.
Technique and why it applies: A finite-state machine is suitable because number validity depends on the order of token categories.
Invariant: state represents the grammar position reached after processing the prefix so far.
Edge cases: Leading/trailing spaces and exponent signs are accepted only in permitted states; empty input ends in an invalid state.
Complexity: No author label was supplied. Time is O(n) and auxiliary space O(1), since each character causes one transition through a fixed table.

Task and constraints: You are given a large integer represented as an integer array digits, where each digits[i] is the i^th digit of the integer. The digits are ordered from most significant to least significant in left-to-right order. The large integer does not contain any leading 0's. The method returns the requested result for the stated input format.
Idea: Scans digits right to left, turns trailing 9s into zeroes, increments the first non-nine digit and returns; if all digits were nine, it prepends 1.
Technique and why it applies: Carry propagation increments a decimal digit array without converting the entire number.
Invariant: All positions to the right of the current index have been reset to zero when a carry continues left.
Edge cases: [1,2,3] becomes [1,2,4], while [9] becomes [1,0]. The first variant mutates digits before returning.
Complexity: No author label was supplied. Time is O(n) worst case; auxiliary space is O(n) only when all digits are 9 and a new leading list is created.
